title: America Has Run Out of EB-2 Green Cards for Indians. The Queue Will Not Move Until October.
excerpt: Every EB-2 visa number allocated to India for the fiscal year has been used. Processing is frozen until the annual reset on October 1, leaving at least 28,000 approved applicants in limbo.
body:
The United States has exhausted its entire allocation of EB-2 immigrant visas for Indian nationals in fiscal year 2026. No new green cards will be issued in the category until the fiscal year resets on October 1 — freezing the applications of tens of thousands of professionals who have already been approved but are stuck waiting for a number that no longer exists.

The EB-2 category covers professionals with advanced degrees or exceptional ability — the engineers, researchers, physicians, and senior technologists who form the backbone of America's skilled immigration pipeline. Indians account for the overwhelming majority of EB-2 demand, and the category's annual allocation typically runs out months before the fiscal year ends.

This year, the freeze arrived in June. The U.S. Department of State had warned it was coming. Its June 2026 Visa Bulletin retrogressed the final action dates for EB-2 India, citing "high demand and number use." The bulletin added that making the category "unavailable" might be necessary — and that is exactly what has happened.

What Frozen Means in Practice

The practical consequences are immediate and blunt. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services will not accept new adjustment of status applications for EB-2 India. It will not process pending ones either. Consular posts abroad will not stamp any EB-2 visas for Indian nationals. Every applicant in the queue stays exactly where they are.

The freeze does not cancel anyone's case. Approved petitions remain valid. Priority dates are preserved. But no one moves forward.

""Recapture unused green cards and prevent future green card waste," Bhutoria has urged, noting that the Department of Homeland Security already has the statutory authority to act."

For the workers themselves, this means another stretch of limbo — unable to change jobs freely, unable to start a business, unable to buy a home without the gnawing uncertainty of temporary status. Many have been in the queue for more than a decade.

The Numbers Behind the Bottleneck

The scale of the backlog is staggering. According to USCIS data from early 2026, there are at least 28,377 pending EB-2 adjustment of status applications from India alone — and that figure is a confirmed minimum. The actual number is higher because several data cells in the government's reporting are suppressed for privacy.

By contrast, China has roughly 6,000 pending EB-2 cases. The rest of the world combined has about 33,000. India's share of the global queue is disproportionate not because Indians file more petitions per capita, but because per-country caps — a feature of the Immigration and Nationality Act — prevent any single country from receiving more than roughly 7 per cent of total employment-based visas in a given year.

The result is a system where an Indian engineer with an approved petition filed in 2014 might still be waiting for a visa number, while an equally qualified applicant from a country with lower demand clears the process in months.

The Reform That Never Arrives

Legislative proposals to eliminate or raise per-country caps have circulated in Congress for years. The most prominent, the Eagle Act, passed the House in 2022 but stalled in the Senate. No comparable bill has gained traction since.

Meanwhile, a member of the President's Advisory Commission on Asian Americans, Ajay Bhutoria, has recommended that the government recapture more than 230,000 unused employment-based green cards from 1992 through 2025 — visa numbers that were allocated but never issued due to bureaucratic delays. Redistributing those numbers could provide immediate relief without changing the annual cap itself.

"Recapture unused green cards and prevent future green card waste," Bhutoria has urged, noting that the Department of Homeland Security already has the statutory authority to act.

So far, the administration has not responded to the proposal.

What Comes Next

The fiscal year resets on October 1. When it does, fresh EB-2 numbers will enter circulation, priority dates will advance, and USCIS will resume processing. The cycle will begin again — and, if history is any guide, the new allocation will be exhausted well before the following September.

For now, the message to the estimated 400,000-plus Indians in the employment-based green card backlog is the same one it has been for years: wait.

The H-1B workers caught in this limbo are not prospective immigrants weighing whether to come to America. They are already here — working, paying taxes, raising children in American schools, and contributing to the companies that define the U.S. technology sector. The system that recruited them is the same system that cannot process them.
